prompt: How many general types of organic reactions does Section 6.1 describe?
explanation: There are four general types of organic reactions: additions, eliminations, substitutions, and rearrangements.

prompt: What are the two broad ways of organizing organic chemical reactions?

choices.text: By what kinds of reactions occur and by how those reactions occur
By whether they are fast or slow
choices.why: Rates come into a reaction's mechanism, but the two ways of organizing reactions are by kind and by how they occur.

choices.text: By whether they happen in the laboratory or in living organisms
choices.why: Both lab and biological reactions fall into the same kinds; the text organizes reactions by what kind they are and how they occur.

choices.text: By the number of carbon atoms in the reactants
choices.why: Reaction types depend on how reactants and products are related, not on the size of the molecules.

explanation: Organic chemical reactions can be organized broadly in two ways: by what kinds of reactions occur (additions, eliminations, substitutions, rearrangements) and by how those reactions occur (their mechanisms, Section 6.2).

prompt: What happens in an addition reaction?

choices.text: Two reactants add together to form a single product with no atoms left over
A single reactant splits into two products
choices.why: That is an elimination, which is in a sense the opposite of an addition.

choices.text: Two reactants exchange parts to give two new products
choices.why: That is a substitution.

choices.text: A single reactant reorganizes its bonds to give an isomer
choices.why: That is a rearrangement.

explanation: Addition reactions occur when two reactants add together to form a single product with no atoms "left over", as when ethylene reacts with HBr to give an alkyl bromide.

prompt: What happens in an elimination reaction?

choices.text: A single reactant splits into two products, often forming a small molecule such as water or HBr
Two reactants combine into one product
choices.why: That is an addition, the opposite of an elimination.
That is a substitution, which starts with two reactants rather than one.

choices.text: A single reactant gives a single isomeric product
choices.why: That is a rearrangement; an elimination gives two products.

explanation: Elimination reactions occur when a single reactant splits into two products, often with the formation of a small molecule such as water or HBr. They are, in a sense, the opposite of addition reactions.

prompt: What happens in a substitution reaction?

choices.text: Two reactants exchange parts to give two new products
Two reactants add together into one product
choices.why: That is an addition. In a substitution, two reactants give two products.

choices.text: One reactant splits into two products
choices.why: That is an elimination, which starts from a single reactant.

choices.text: One reactant is converted into an isomer
choices.why: That is a rearrangement.

explanation: Substitution reactions occur when two reactants exchange parts to give two new products, as when methyl acetate reacts with water to give acetic acid and methanol.

prompt: What is the product of a rearrangement reaction?

choices.text: An isomer of the single reactant, formed by a reorganization of bonds and atoms
Two smaller molecules, one of them often water
choices.why: Splitting into two products is an elimination. A rearrangement gives one product with the same formula as the reactant.

choices.text: A single product made from two reactants
choices.why: That is an addition; a rearrangement starts from only one reactant.

choices.text: Two new products made by exchanging parts between two reactants
choices.why: That is a substitution.

explanation: Rearrangement reactions occur when a single reactant undergoes a reorganization of bonds and atoms to yield an isomeric product.

prompt: Which kind of reaction is, in a sense, the opposite of an addition reaction?

choices.why: A substitution exchanges parts between two reactants; it doesn't undo an addition.
A rearrangement turns one reactant into one isomeric product; nothing is added or removed.
Eliminations split one reactant into two products, the reverse of two reactants combining into one.

explanation: In an addition, two reactants combine into a single product; in an elimination, a single reactant splits into two products. Elimination reactions are therefore, in a sense, the opposite of addition reactions.

prompt: Ethylene, H2C=CH2, undergoes an addition reaction with HBr. What forms?

choices.why: Swapping an H for a Br and releasing a second product would be a substitution. In an addition, no atoms are left over.
An addition gives a single product; both reactants end up in it together.
This product has two Br atoms and has lost H; adding HBr puts one H and one Br on the two carbons.

explanation: In an addition, two reactants add together to form a single product with no atoms left over. Ethylene and HBr give the alkyl bromide bromoethane, CH3CH2Br.

prompt: With an acid catalyst, ethanol reacts as CH3CH2OH ⟶ H2C=CH2 + H2O. What kind of reaction is this?

choices.why: The acid is only a catalyst. One reactant gives two products, which is the opposite of an addition.
A substitution needs two reactants exchanging parts; here a single reactant splits apart.
A rearrangement gives one isomeric product, but here a small molecule, water, is split off.

explanation: A single reactant, the alcohol ethanol, splits into two products, ethylene and water. Eliminations often form a small molecule such as water, as in this acid-catalyzed reaction of an alcohol to give an alkene.

prompt: With an acid catalyst, methyl acetate reacts with water: CH3CO2CH3 + H2O ⟶ CH3CO2H + CH3OH. What kind of reaction is this?

choices.why: Water is a reactant, but there are two products. An addition gives a single product with no atoms left over.
An elimination starts from one reactant; here two reactants are involved.
A rearrangement converts a single reactant into an isomer; here two reactants give two different products.

explanation: The ester and water exchange parts to give two new products, a carboxylic acid (acetic acid) and an alcohol (methanol), so this is a substitution. Similar reactions occur in the metabolism of dietary fats.

prompt: In glycolysis, dihydroxyacetone phosphate is converted into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. What kind of reaction is this, and why?

choices.text: A rearrangement, because the single product is a constitutional isomer of the single reactant
An elimination, because a phosphate is lost
choices.why: Both compounds carry the phosphate. Nothing is split off; the bonds and atoms are reorganized.

choices.text: A substitution, because a group is exchanged
choices.why: A substitution needs two reactants exchanging parts; here there is one reactant and one product.

choices.text: An addition, because the product is a single molecule
choices.why: An addition makes one product from two reactants. Here there is only one reactant.

explanation: Rearrangement reactions occur when a single reactant undergoes a reorganization of bonds and atoms to yield an isomeric product. Dihydroxyacetone phosphate gives its constitutional isomer glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, a step in the glycolysis pathway.

prompt: Classify the reaction CH3CH=CH2 + Br2 ⟶ CH3CHBrCH2Br.

choices.why: Nothing is exchanged and no second product forms; both bromine atoms end up in the single product.
An elimination splits one reactant into two products. Here two reactants combine into one.
The product contains Br atoms the reactant didn't have, so it is not an isomer of the starting alkene.

explanation: Two reactants, the alkene and Br2, add together to form a single product with no atoms left over, so this is an addition.

choices.why: This is the reverse of an addition: one reactant gives two products rather than two reactants giving one.
There is only one reactant, so nothing can exchange parts with it.
A rearrangement gives a single isomeric product, but here HCl is split off as a second product.

explanation: A single reactant splits into two products, an alkene and the small molecule HCl, so this is an elimination.

prompt: Classify the reaction CH3CH2CH2Br + NaI ⟶ CH3CH2CH2I + NaBr.

choices.why: There are two products, not one, so the reactants haven't simply added together.
An elimination starts from a single reactant and usually forms a double bond; here two reactants swap Br and I.
The organic product contains I instead of Br, so it is not an isomer of the reactant.

explanation: The two reactants exchange parts (Br for I) to give two new products, so this is a substitution.

choices.why: Nothing is added: reactant and product are both C4H8.
No small molecule is split off; there is only one product.
A substitution needs two reactants exchanging parts; here a single reactant reorganizes.

explanation: A single reactant gives a single product with the same formula, C4H8, but with the double bond in a different place. A reorganization of bonds and atoms that yields an isomeric product is a rearrangement.
